paras: The lynching of an unnamed Black man at Oxford, Mississippi, took place in or shortly before early August 1885, after he was accused of having "attempted an outrage." It is known only from a one-sentence item in a Tennessee weekly, which gave no name, date, perpetrators or method.

According to the only report found, a Black man said to have attempted an "outrage," the period's term for a sexual assault, at Oxford, Miss., was lynched. The item does not say who the alleged victim of the attempt was, whether the man had been arrested, how many people took part in the killing, or how he was killed.
No report of an inquest, arrests or official response appears in the coverage.

The Pulaski Citizen of Pulaski, Tennessee, printed the news on 6 August 1885 as a single line: "A negro who attempted an outrage at Oxford, Miss., was lynched." The sentence identified the man only by race, stated the accusation as fact rather than as a charge, and offered no comment on the killing. No fuller local or wire account and no Black-press report of the episode were found for August and September 1885.
